defaults.permitted_development: Across Suffolk, a modest roof-light on a house is usually permitted development if it projects no more than 150mm from the existing roof slope, does not exceed the height of the existing roof and the property still benefits from normal householder rights. Planning permission becomes more likely where the work is on a listed building, in a controlled area or tied to a wider roof enlargement.

rules.height_rules: Across Suffolk, the roof-light should not make any part of the roof higher than it is now. A low-profile installation that leaves the original roof form dominant is generally the strongest option.
rules.depth_rules: Across Suffolk, the unit must not project more than 150 millimetres from the plane of the existing roof slope. Once the projection starts to read as a box, dormer or raised roof feature, the simpler roof-light route usually stops applying.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Suffolk, boundary impact usually comes through privacy rather than distance. Side-facing roof-light windows should be obscure-glazed and, if openable, the opening part should have its lowest point at least 1.7 metres above the room floor.
rules.roof_rules: Across Suffolk, the proposal should read as a modest alteration to the existing roof rather than a new roof form in its own right. Roof terraces and larger enlargements are separate development types with stricter rules.
rules.materials_rules: Across Suffolk, use flashings, frame colours and glazing details that sit quietly within the existing roof. The closer the finish is to the host roof covering and the less bulky the frame, the easier it is to keep the alteration visually subordinate.

restrictions.conservation_area: A roof-light in a conservation area is usually easiest to justify when it is discreetly placed and does not disrupt an established roof form.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building consent may be required for roof-lights where the work alters historic roof fabric, framing, coverings or the character of the building.
restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the standard roof-light allowance survives everywhere: Article 4 controls and site-specific conditions can require an application for visible roof changes.

rules.permitted_development: For houses in East Suffolk, the usual roof-light route is to keep the unit modest: no more than 150mm projection from the existing roof slope and no increase above the existing roof height. Once the proposal sits on a more sensitive roofscape or forms part of a larger roof alteration, planning permission is more likely to be needed.

rules.height_rules: A roof-light must not push the roof above the existing highest part. Keeping the frame low-profile and subordinate to the roof slope is usually the safest approach.
rules.depth_rules: Keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: Roof-lights do not have a normal setback rule, but side-facing windows can still affect neighbours. Obscure glazing and a 1.7 metre minimum level to any opening part are the usual privacy conditions.
rules.roof_rules: Think of a roof-light as a small insertion into the existing slope, not as a way to reshape the roof. Larger additions, terraces and platforms are outside the ordinary roof-light allowance.
rules.materials_rules: Choose a roof-light that feels recessive rather than attention-seeking. Simple frame colours, tidy flashings and detailing that works with the existing roof covering generally give the strongest planning outcome.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even small roof-lights can need closer scrutiny if they are proposed on prominent slopes or on buildings with a consistent historic roofscape.
restrictions.listed_building: A listed building roof usually needs a heritage-led approach: even a small roof-light can require consent if it affects the historic fabric or appearance.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions or roof-specific planning conditions can remove the usual householder right to add roof-lights, especially on visible elevations or in heritage areas.

rules.permitted_development: In Mid Suffolk, a simple skylight or roof-light is commonly permitted development provided it remains a minor roof alteration, projects no more than 150mm from the slope and does not exceed the roof's existing height. Heritage controls, local restrictions and larger roof changes can all take the work outside that simpler route.

rules.height_rules: Height control for a roof-light is simple but strict: the proposal should not rise above the existing roof. The more flush and subordinate the unit appears, the easier the scheme is to keep within the normal householder route.
rules.depth_rules: Keep the projection tight to the existing slope. The normal roof-light limit is 150mm, and anything noticeably prouder than that risks being treated as a more substantial roof alteration.
rules.boundary_rules: If the proposal creates a side-facing window, it should be obscure-glazed and any opening part should have its lowest edge at least 1.7 metres above the floor level of the room. Privacy and visible road-facing roof slopes deserve the earliest check.
rules.roof_rules: A roof-light is easiest to defend when it remains subordinate to the slope and does not slide into dormer or terrace territory. Once the wider roof form changes materially, the normal roof-light route no longer tells the full story.
rules.materials_rules: Use flashings, frame colours and glazing details that sit quietly within the existing roof. The closer the finish is to the host roof covering and the less bulky the frame, the easier it is to keep the alteration visually subordinate.
